extracted.intended_audience: writers, orators, and students of rhetoric seeking to produce 'sublime' prose or speech
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing elevated, persuasive, and majestic prose/speech (the classical notion of the Sublime). Covers diction, rhythm, figures (metaphor/hyperbole), composition/unity, and how art should serve natural genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity outweighs correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness (sublimity) redeems mistakes; the faults of truly great writers are negligible compared with their merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘While they are far from unerring, yet they are all more than human...each of these great men again and again redeems all his mistakes by a single touch of sublimity and true excellence.’ Scoring note: prioritize signs of grandeur and elevating power over minor technical faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature vs Art — let art assist nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity springs from natural genius, whereas correctness (art) is due to skill; the ideal is for art to assist and perfect nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Since the merit of impeccable correctness is, generally speaking, due to art, and sublimity, though not sustained, to genius, it is proper that art should always assist Nature.’ Practical implication: refine natural power with craft rather than substituting craft for feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for grandeur and the unusual
rubrics_metrics.description: Human admiration is drawn to the vast, great, and unusual rather than to the merely useful or small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: we admire the Nile or a volcano more than a small stream or a domestic fire. In composition, favor images and ideas that evoke largeness, awe, and the extraordinary rather than mundane utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphor, illustration, and imagery judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors, illustration and imagery are closely akin and are essential instruments of sublimity when properly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce metaphors naturally and make sure they arise from feeling or situation rather than appear forced. The chapter treats them as central contributors to elevation; avoid laboured or irrelevant images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole must be concealed and emotionally grounded
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The best hyperbole is the one which conceals the very fact of its being a hyperbole.’ Hyperbole is credible when it arises naturally from intense emotion or striking incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thucydides and Herodotus make hyperbole believable because it flows from events (e.g. 'a drink of mud and gore yet worth fighting for'). Anti-pattern: obvious, advertising hyperbole that undermines credibility (Isocrates's puerility). Avoid overshooting the mark, which causes the passage to sag or produce the opposite effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of words (melody) produces grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is a kind of melody in words; the rhythmic arrangement of phrases moves hearers and creates majestic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cadence, piling of phrase on phrase, and rhythmic variation to 'build up one majestic whole.' The use of certain metrical feet (e.g., dactyls) or cadences contributes to grandeur. Delivery and rhythm can make commonplace words majestic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer robust rhythms (dactyls/spondees) for dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dactyls and long rhythmic feet (spondees) contribute to the sense of grandeur; mutilating such rhythm (cutting syllables) weakens sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: specific metrical examples show that the first foot being long is crucial for resonance. Practical rule: preserve rhythmic weight in key phrases; be wary of shortening or lengthening beats that upset the cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unify members and bind by rhythm (structural unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The separate effects of grandeur must be united into a single system and embraced by bonds of rhythm so the period has organic unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: as body parts form an organism, sentence members should interlock. If grand effects are separated, sublimity is scattered. Aim for periods where parts support each other and the whole has a living voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weak, agitated, or over-rhythmic meters
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak rhythms (pyrrhics, trochees) or over-rhythmical passages become merely pretty, cheap, and dance-like, diverting attention to rhythm rather than thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: passages that produce a monotonous jingle or make the audience 'keep time with their feet.' Avoid excessive light feet and too regular, sing-song rhythm in elevated passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control sentence length: avoid extreme concision and prolixity
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme conciseness mutilates grandeur by over-compression; excessive prolixity makes passages drag and lose life. True brevity goes straight to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish proper compression (concise but full) from injurious shortness (chopped-up, broken fragments). Arrange members to form rounded periods rather than a string of clipped clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elevated diction; avoid trivial and colloquial words
rubrics_metrics.description: Trivial, colloquial, or paltry words degrade an otherwise grand passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Herodotus's 'seething', 'flagged', and 'unpleasing' are cited as unworthy in a sublime description. Prefer dignified, fitting words; replace or recast commonplace terms that jar with the subject's magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal sordid or base details; fit words to the subject's dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid explicit, contemptible, or sordid particulars in elevated passages—Nature conceals ignoble parts; the writer should too, except under necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to art: do not lay bare what spoils the beauty of the whole. If necessary (extreme necessity), handle base matters with tact and place them in the background rather than foregrounding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use composition (verbal carpentry) to elevate ordinary language
rubrics_metrics.description: Even writers not sublime by nature can achieve dignity and grandeur by force of composition and skillful arrangement of common language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Philistus, Aristophanes occasionally, and Euripides gain grandeur via composition. Practical implication: good sentence architecture, cadence, and apt placement can ennoble otherwise vulgar phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic and pause effects: exploit consonant clashes and pauses for austerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consonant clashes and well-placed pauses ('words offer resistance to each other') can produce an austere, stable grandeur by delaying pronunciation and planting phrases with dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use harsher consonant groupings sparingly to produce weight; ensure pauses occur where they support organic unity rather than interrupting it. The effect depends on the interaction of sound and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange details to sustain crescendo; avoid untimely mundane specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not insert trivial, domestic, or shop-like details amid a grand description; such untimeliness destroys the intended effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Theopompus's mixing of 'bags and spices and sacks' with gold and jewels degrades the scene. Remedies: group mundane items under a tasteful collective phrase, or place specifics so they do not interrupt a rising sweep of description.
